definition: A joint between two structural members made using bolts. One of the two main connection types in steelwork (the other being welded). Can be assembled on site without specialist equipment.
A joint formed by melting metal at the interface between two members to fuse them together. Typically done in a fabrication workshop and creates a very strong, rigid joint.
A connection designed to transfer bending moment from one member to another, as well as shear and axial forces. It keeps the angle between members fixed - the members behave as if continuous.
A connection that transfers shear and axial forces but deliberately allows rotation. Think of it as a hinge - the members can rotate relative to each other, so no bending moment is transferred.
A fully restrained connection that transfers all forces and moments. The angle between connected members does not change under load. Also called a 'fixed' connection.

A connection between a pinned and rigid connection - it transfers some bending moment but also allows some rotation. Most real connections behave semi-rigidly, though they are often simplified in design.
A connection designed primarily to transfer vertical shear force. It does not resist bending moment, so the beam end is free to rotate. Common for simply-supported beams.

A connection that joins two lengths of the same member end-to-end - for example, joining two column sections one above the other. Used when a member is too long to fabricate or transport in one piece.
A simple shear connection where a flat plate is welded to the supporting member (e.g. a column) and bolted to the web of the beam. Quick and cheap to fabricate and erect.
A plate welded to the end of a beam which is then bolted to the face of a column or another beam. Can be designed as a shear-only or moment connection depending on plate size and bolt arrangement.
A connection using two angle sections (cleats) bolted to both the beam web and the supporting member. One of the oldest and most traditional simple connection types in steelwork.
Similar to an angle cleat but using a flat plate bolted to the beam web. Transfers shear load only.
A moment connection where plates are bolted or welded to the flanges of a beam to transfer bending moment to a column. The flanges carry the moment and the web carries the shear.
A connection specifically designed to withstand earthquake forces. Must be ductile - able to absorb energy through deformation without fracturing.
A connection configuration that has been tested and approved by a design code (e.g. AISC) for use in seismic zones without the need for project-specific testing.
The connection at the bottom of a column to the foundation. Usually a steel base plate sitting on a concrete pad, anchored down with anchor bolts.
A triangular steel plate added to the bottom of a beam near a moment connection to deepen the section and increase its stiffness and moment capacity at the joint.
A flat steel plate used to connect bracing members, trusses, or other structural members to beams or columns. Acts as a hub that distributes load between members.
A bolt used to connect a steel structure to a concrete foundation. Transfers loads from the steel into the concrete below. The most common way to fix a column base to a foundation.
An anchor installed in wet concrete before it sets. Because it is embedded during casting, it bonds mechanically with the concrete for very high load capacity.
An anchor installed into hardened, existing concrete by drilling a hole. Either mechanical (expansion) or chemical (adhesive). Used when the concrete is already cast.
A post-installed anchor where adhesive (resin) is injected into a drilled hole and a threaded rod or rebar is inserted. The resin cures to create a strong bond. Also called an adhesive anchor.
A post-installed mechanical anchor that grips concrete by expanding against the walls of a drilled hole when tightened. Works by friction. Less strong than chemical anchors in cracked concrete.
A short steel rod with a head welded to a steel beam to create composite action with a concrete slab above. The head provides the mechanical interlock that transfers shear between steel and concrete.
A steel plate cast into a concrete element with anchors attached to it. Provides a steel face to which other steel members can be welded or bolted after the concrete is cast.
A C-shaped steel channel cast into concrete, allowing bolts to be slid along it and tightened at any position. Used for cladding and façade fixings where exact bolt positions are uncertain.
A post-installed anchor that relies on a mechanical interlock created by cutting an undercut shape in the concrete hole. Very high load capacity, used in cracked concrete.
A cement-based material poured under a base plate after erection to fill the gap between the plate and the concrete foundation. Ensures even bearing and transfers load uniformly.
Another name for anchor bolts used to hold down a column base. The term 'holding down' emphasises their role in resisting uplift as well as shear.
A high-strength bolt used to join structural steel members. Unlike standard hardware bolts, structural bolts are manufactured to tight tolerances and come in defined grades.

A number indicating a bolt's strength. The first number is 1/100 of the tensile strength (MPa); the second is 10 times the yield-to-tensile ratio. E.g. grade 8.8: tensile strength 800 MPa, yield at 80% of that.
The most common grade of structural bolt. Tensile strength of 800 MPa. Used in the majority of standard steelwork connections.
A higher-strength bolt with tensile strength of 1000 MPa. Used in high-load connections or when bolt size needs to be kept small.

High Strength Friction Grip bolt. Tightened to a very precise tension so the clamping force between the plates creates friction that transfers load. The bolt itself does not bear against the hole. Used in slip-critical connections.

A bolted connection where load is transferred by friction between the contact surfaces rather than bolt bearing. Requires HSFG bolts tightened to a specified pretension. Used where slip would be unacceptable.
A standard bolted connection where the bolt shank bears against the hole edge to transfer load. Simpler and cheaper than friction connections but allows a small slip at first loading.
The cutting force acting on a bolt across its cross-section. A bolt in shear is being pushed to one side on one face and the other side on the other face - like scissors cutting through it.
Force pulling a bolt along its length (trying to stretch it). Bolts in moment connections often experience tension as the connection tries to rotate and pull the flanges apart.
The most common weld type, forming a triangular cross-section in the corner between two members. Used to join overlapping or perpendicular surfaces. Simpler and cheaper than a butt weld.
A weld that joins two members end-to-end in the same plane, filling the gap between them. A full-penetration butt weld is as strong as the parent material itself.
A butt weld that penetrates the full thickness of the connected material. Develops the full strength of the base metal. More expensive than partial penetration.
A butt weld that does not penetrate the full thickness. Cheaper but lower capacity - cannot develop the full strength of the base metal.
The leg length of a fillet weld, or the throat depth of a butt weld. A larger weld size means greater capacity but more material and heat input.

The shortest distance from the root of a weld to its face - the critical dimension for weld strength calculations. For a standard equal-leg fillet weld, the throat = 0.707 × leg length (for a 45° weld geometry). Weld resistance is calculated per unit length of throat.
A flat disc placed under a bolt head or nut to distribute the clamping load over a larger area and prevent damage to the connected surface.
The threaded female component that engages with a bolt thread. Tightening the nut draws the bolt into tension and clamps the connected parts together.
A process that welds headed studs directly to a steel beam using an electric arc, typically to create composite action with a concrete slab.
A pulling force that tries to stretch a member along its length. A rope under load is in pure tension. Steel is very strong in tension.
A pushing force that tries to shorten a member along its length. A column carrying the weight of a building is in compression.
A force acting across (perpendicular to) a member, trying to cut it in two. Like the action of scissors. Beams experience shear due to the vertical loads they carry.

The internal force that causes a beam or column to bend. It is the product of a force multiplied by the distance from the point of interest. A long, loaded beam experiences high bending moments in its middle.
A twisting force - a moment that tries to rotate a member about its own axis. Like wringing out a towel. Torsion is more complex than bending and often avoided in design.
A force acting along the length (axis) of a member - either tension (pulling) or compression (pushing).
Another term for axial force - a force acting perpendicular to a surface or along a member's axis.
The compressive force between two surfaces in contact - for example, between a bolt shank and the edge of a bolt hole, or between a base plate and a concrete foundation.
A localised shear failure that can occur in a concrete slab or column base when a concentrated load punches through like a cookie cutter. Critical for column-to-slab connections.

An additional tensile force in a bolt caused by the lever action of a bending plate. When a plate deforms under load it 'pries' on the bolt, increasing the bolt tension beyond what simple calculation suggests.
The permanent, constant weight of the structure itself - steel beams, concrete slabs, cladding. It never changes. Also called permanent load in Eurocode.
Forces from the occupants, furniture, and moveable equipment in a building. It varies over time. Also called imposed load or variable load.
Lateral and uplift forces applied to a structure by wind pressure and suction. Buildings must be designed to resist wind in all directions.
Forces generated in a structure during an earthquake by ground movement causing the structure to accelerate. Requires special design considerations for ductility.
Loads from the use and occupancy of a structure - people, furniture, vehicles. The Eurocode term for live load.
A concentrated force acting at a single location. For example, a column sitting on a beam applies a point load at that location.
A load spread over a length or area rather than concentrated at one point. For example, the self-weight of a beam is a uniformly distributed load along its length.
The force exerted by a support on a structure in response to the applied loads. At a simple support, the reaction is vertical; at a fixed support, there are also horizontal and moment reactions.
A set of rules specifying which loads must be applied together for design. Different combinations apply for different limit states. The most onerous combination governs the design.
The factored load used in structural calculations. It equals the characteristic load multiplied by a partial safety factor, and is used to check structural capacity at the ultimate limit state.

A statistically defined value of a load, used as the reference value before safety factors are applied. For variable loads (wind, imposed), it typically corresponds to a value with a 50-year return period (2% annual probability of exceedance). For permanent loads (self-weight), it is usually the mean value.
The weight of the structural members themselves. Always present and must be accounted for in design.
A measure of how much a structure resists deformation when loaded. A stiff structure deflects little; a flexible one deflects a lot. Measured as force per unit displacement.

The ability of a material or structure to undergo large deformations before fracturing. Ductility is crucial in seismic design - a ductile structure absorbs energy through controlled deformation rather than sudden collapse.
The property of a material that allows it to return to its original shape after a load is removed. Elastic behaviour is reversible - no permanent deformation occurs.
The behaviour of a material after it has been stressed beyond its yield point. Plastic deformation is permanent - the material does not spring back when the load is removed.

The stress at which a material begins to deform permanently (plastically). For structural steel this is a key design parameter - members are typically designed to stay below yield under service loads.
The maximum stress a material can withstand before fracturing. Higher than yield strength. The difference between yield and ultimate is the material's 'reserve' strength.
A sudden sideways failure of a slender member under compression. Instead of squashing, the member bows sideways. Long, thin columns and beam webs are prone to buckling.

A buckling mode in which an unrestrained beam deflects laterally and twists simultaneously under load. The compression flange acts like a strut and buckles sideways. Prevented by lateral restraints (purlins, floor slabs) that brace the compression flange. Critical for long, deep, unrestrained beams.
Buckling of a thin plate element within a section (e.g. the web or flange of an I-beam) rather than the member as a whole. Prevented by limiting plate slenderness.
The movement of a structure or member from its original position under load. Beams sag; columns sway. Deflection limits are set by serviceability requirements.
A change in shape or size of a structural member under load. Includes both elastic (recoverable) and plastic (permanent) deformation.
The internal force per unit area within a material. Measured in megapascals (MPa) or N/mm². There are normal stresses (tension/compression) and shear stresses.
The deformation of a material expressed as a fraction of its original dimension. Strain = change in length ÷ original length. Dimensionless (no units).

A location in a structure where the full plastic moment capacity (Mp) has been reached. The section continues to rotate at constant moment - behaving like a frictionless pin for additional rotation. Plastic analysis allows load to redistribute through a sequence of plastic hinge formations before collapse.
The ratio of applied load to design capacity, expressed as a decimal or percentage. A ratio of 1.0 (or 100%) means the member is exactly at capacity. Ratios above 1.0 indicate overstress.
A multiplier applied to loads or divider applied to capacities to ensure a structure has adequate reserve strength beyond its design load.

A factor applied to loads (γF) or material strengths (γM) in limit state design to account for uncertainty. For example, in Eurocode, dead load is typically factored by γG = 1.35 and steel yield strength is divided by γM0 = 1.0 at ULS. Partial factors replace the old single global safety factor.

In an indeterminate structure, the shift of bending moment from sections that have reached their plastic moment capacity to less-stressed sections. Allows a more economical design than elastic analysis. Limited by Eurocode to prevent excessive plastic rotation damaging serviceability.

Sudden failure of a material by the propagation of a crack. Unlike ductile failure, fracture is abrupt and without warning. Brittle fracture is a particular concern in cold weather with certain steel grades.
Progressive weakening of a material under repeated cyclic loading. A small crack can grow with each load cycle until failure occurs at a stress far below the static strength.
The slow, time-dependent deformation of a material under sustained load. Most significant in concrete, especially under compressive loading at elevated temperatures.
A form of steel specifically produced to consistent mechanical properties for use in construction. Key properties: high strength, ductility, and weldability.
A structural steel grade with a nominal yield strength of 235 MPa. The 'S' denotes structural, '235' is the yield strength. Used for lightly loaded members and in older structures.
Structural steel with a nominal yield strength of 275 MPa. The standard grade for most UK and European structural steelwork.
Structural steel with a nominal yield strength of 355 MPa. Higher strength than S275, allowing smaller sections. Common for heavily loaded structures.
High-strength structural steels with yield strengths of 420 and 460 MPa. Used in long-span structures or where weight saving is critical. Require more care in welding.
Concrete strengthened by embedding steel bars (rebar) or mesh within it. Concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension; the steel carries the tensile forces.
Steel bar embedded in concrete to carry tensile forces. Commonly known as rebar. Ribbed bars are standard - the ribs improve the bond between steel and concrete.
A designation indicating the compressive strength of concrete. E.g. C25/30 means a cylinder strength of 25 MPa and a cube strength of 30 MPa. Higher classes for more highly loaded elements.
Construction where steel and concrete work together as a combined structural system, each contributing what it does best. Steel beams with concrete slabs on top, connected by shear studs.
A steel section (I-beam, channel, angle) formed by pushing hot steel through shaped rollers. The most common way to produce standard steel sections.
A steel section formed at room temperature by bending thin sheet steel. Lighter and thinner than hot-rolled sections. Used for purlins, cladding rails, and light structures.
Steel sections with a hollow, closed cross-section - circular (CHS), rectangular (RHS), or square (SHS). Very efficient for columns and members carrying both bending and torsion.
A corrosion-protection process where steel is coated with zinc by dipping it in molten zinc. The zinc corrodes preferentially, protecting the steel underneath.

[1st Generation Eurocode] A set of European design standards for structural engineering, covering concrete (EC2), steel (EC3), composite (EC4), and other materials. Used across the EU and many other countries.
[1st Generation Eurocode] Eurocode 3 - the design standard for steel structures. Part 1-8 specifically covers the design of joints and connections in steel.
[1st Generation Eurocode] Eurocode 4 - the design standard for composite steel-concrete structures. Covers beams, columns, slabs, and connections in composite construction.
[1st Generation Eurocode] Eurocode 2 - the design standard for concrete structures. Covers the design of reinforced and prestressed concrete elements.
The American Institute of Steel Construction specification for structural steel buildings. The primary US code for steel design, widely used internationally.
A design condition representing structural failure - collapse, fracture, or overturning. Structure is designed so that applied loads do not exceed capacity at ULS. Safety factors are highest here.
A design condition relating to the normal use of the structure - excessive deflection, vibration, or cracking. Not about collapse but about whether the structure performs satisfactorily in use.
A country-specific supplement to a Eurocode that sets the values of nationally determined parameters (safety factors, load values, etc.) for use in that country.
A value of a material property or load with a defined low probability of being exceeded. For material strength, typically the 5th percentile (only 5% of samples are weaker).
A characteristic value divided by (or multiplied by) a partial safety factor. Used in ULS calculations. Accounts for uncertainty in material properties and loads.
Verification that a structural element or connection satisfies all the relevant criteria in a design code. IDEA StatiCa performs code checks automatically using FEA results.
A horizontal structural member that primarily carries loads by bending. Transfers load from slabs and other elements to columns or walls.
A vertical structural member that primarily carries load in compression (axial force). Transfers load from beams down to foundations.
Diagonal members added to a structural frame to resist horizontal loads (wind, seismic). Bracing works by forming triangles within the frame, which are inherently rigid.
A structural framework made of straight members arranged in triangles. Very efficient for spanning long distances. The top and bottom chords carry bending; the diagonals and verticals carry shear.
A horizontal beam running along the length of a roof, spanning between rafters or portal frames. Supports the roof cladding and provides lateral restraint to the rafters.
A sloping roof beam running from the ridge to the eave. In a portal frame building, the rafter is the sloping part of the frame.
A structural system consisting of columns and rafters rigidly connected at their joints, forming a 'portal' shape. Extremely common for industrial buildings and warehouses.
A flat steel plate welded to the bottom of a column and bolted to the foundation. Spreads the column load over the larger area of the concrete foundation.
A plate welded to a beam web or column web to prevent local buckling and distribute concentrated loads. Common at connection points and under point loads.
The vertical plate of an I-section or H-section connecting the two flanges. Primarily resists shear force.

The horizontal plates at the top and bottom of an I-section or H-section. Primarily resist bending moment - the top flange is in compression and the bottom flange is in tension for a simply-supported beam.
The classic cross-section shape for steel beams (Universal Beam) and columns (Universal Column). Efficient because material is concentrated in the flanges where bending stresses are highest.
An L-shaped steel section with two legs. Used for bracing members, cleats, and small secondary members.
A C-shaped steel section. Used for secondary beams, purlins, and connection components.
A round hollow steel tube. Very efficient for compression and torsion. Often used for columns and bracing in architecturally exposed structures.
A square or rectangular hollow steel tube. Good for columns and members subject to bending in one direction.

A computational method that divides a complex structure into thousands of small elements and calculates the stresses, strains, and deformations in each one. Allows very detailed analysis of complex connections.

Component-Based Finite Element Method - the analysis method used by IDEA StatiCa. Combines the speed and transparency of component-based design with the accuracy of finite element analysis. Gives detailed stress maps of connections.
A structural analysis that assumes all materials remain within their elastic range. Stresses are proportional to strains (Hooke's Law). Conservative but simple.
A structural analysis that allows materials to yield and form plastic hinges, enabling load redistribution. Allows a more economic design but requires careful attention to ductility.
Analysis that accounts for changes in stiffness as the structure deforms or as material yields. More accurate than linear analysis for large deformations and post-yield behaviour.
Geometrically and Materially Nonlinear Analysis with Imperfections. The most rigorous buckling analysis method in Eurocode. Accounts for real-world initial imperfections in the geometry.

A 'Discontinuity Region' - a zone in a concrete or steel structure where the normal beam theory assumptions break down. Examples: near supports, openings, and concentrated loads. Requires special analysis (e.g. strut-and-tie).
A 'Bernoulli Region' where standard beam theory applies - plane sections remain plane. The bulk of a beam span is a B-region.
A simplified model for analysing D-regions in concrete. The complex stress field is idealised as a truss of compression struts (concrete) and tension ties (reinforcement).
A localised increase in stress around a geometric discontinuity - a hole, notch, or sharp corner. Stress concentrations are a common cause of fatigue cracking.

A scalar stress measure that combines all six stress components (three direct + three shear) into a single equivalent value for comparison with yield strength. Derived from the von Mises yield criterion. In FEA, contour plots of von Mises stress immediately show where the material has yielded (where the value exceeds fy).
The maximum and minimum direct stresses at a point, acting on planes where shear stress is zero. FEA results are often presented as principal stresses.
The permanent (irrecoverable) deformation remaining after a load is removed. In CBFEM, plastic strain in a connection is limited to ensure the connection does not deform excessively.
The condition where all forces and moments acting on a structure or part of it are balanced - net force and net moment are zero. Fundamental to all structural analysis.

The way a structure is attached to its foundations or supporting structure. Common types: pin (allows rotation), fixed (resists rotation), roller (allows horizontal movement). These determine how loads are transferred.
A sketch showing an isolated part of a structure with all the external forces and reactions acting on it. The essential first step in hand calculations.
A structure where all reactions and internal forces can be found using only the three equations of equilibrium. Simple beams and trusses are usually determinate.
A structure with more unknowns than equilibrium equations. Needs additional compatibility equations to solve. Most real structures are indeterminate - continuous beams, frames, etc.
In structural engineering, a redundant member or reaction is one that is not strictly needed for equilibrium but adds alternative load paths. Redundancy improves structural robustness.
The ability of a structure to withstand accidental or unexpected events (e.g. a vehicle impact, explosion) without disproportionate collapse. Achieved through tying, continuity, and redundancy.
A catastrophic failure mode where local damage (e.g. loss of a column) triggers a cascade of failures throughout the structure. Prevented by good tying and robust design.
The distance between supports of a beam or slab. Longer spans require deeper, heavier sections.

A dimensionless measure of a compression member's susceptibility to buckling: Slenderness = effective length / radius of gyration (λ = Lcr / i). A high slenderness indicates a slender column prone to buckling at a stress well below yield. Eurocode uses a normalised slenderness λ̄ to define buckling curves.

The length of an equivalent pin-ended strut that would buckle at the same load as the real member with its actual end conditions. A pin-pin column: Leff = L. A fixed-fixed column: Leff = 0.5L. A fixed-free (flagpole) column: Leff = 2L. Effective length is the key parameter in column buckling calculations.
A property of a cross-section that measures how far the material is distributed from the centroid. Used in buckling calculations: higher radius of gyration = more buckling resistance.
A geometric property of a cross-section used to calculate bending stress. Stress = Bending Moment ÷ Section Modulus. A larger section modulus means lower stress for the same moment.

A geometric property of a cross-section, also called the moment of inertia (symbol I), measuring how the area is distributed about the bending axis. Higher I means more bending stiffness and lower bending stress for the same moment. I = ∫y²dA. Measured in mm⁴ or cm⁴.

The geometric centre of a cross-section - the point where the section would balance if supported. For doubly symmetric sections, bending stresses are zero at the centroid; for asymmetric sections, the neutral axis (where bending stress is zero) may not coincide with the centroid.
The line in a beam cross-section where bending stress is zero. Above it the material is in compression; below it in tension (for a sagging beam).
A beam that bends concave downward (curves like a hump). The top is in tension and the bottom in compression. Typical over a continuous support.
A beam that bends concave upward (curves like a sag). The top is in compression and the bottom in tension. Typical in the span between supports.
The area of floor or roof that a member (beam, column) is responsible for supporting. Used to calculate the load applied to that member.
The route that loads travel through a structure from where they are applied to where they are resisted (usually the foundations). Understanding load paths is fundamental to structural design.
Bolts cast into or drilled into a concrete foundation to secure a steel base plate. They resist uplift, shear, and overturning forces at the column base.
A joint between two or more steel structural members, transferring forces between them. Can be bolted, welded, or a combination of both.
'HSS' always uppercase (Hollow Structural Section). 'connection' lowercase.
A structural joint connecting a steel member to a timber or glulam element, typically using bolts, screws, or epoxy anchors. Used in hybrid construction where steel and timber elements share loads.
A connection or interface between a steel member and a concrete element. Requires special consideration for load transfer mechanisms including bearing, friction, and anchors.

A connection between a steel element and glued laminated timber (glulam). Commonly achieved with bolted plates, epoxy rods, or hidden fasteners. Requires careful detailing for moisture and fire exposure.

A method of permanently joining steel elements by fusing them with heat, typically from an electric arc. Welds are classified by type (fillet, butt, full-penetration) and designed to transfer forces between connected parts.

A threaded fastener used to connect structural elements. Structural bolts are typically high-strength grades (8.8 or 10.9) and may be designed to resist shear, tension, or combined loading depending on the connection type.
A deep beam built up by welding or bolting plates together - typically two flanges and a web - rather than rolled as a single section. Used for very long spans or heavy loads.

A composite floor system comprising a profiled steel deck acting as permanent formwork for a concrete slab. When shear connectors are provided, the deck acts compositely with the concrete to increase stiffness and capacity.

A zone in a structure where the assumption that plane sections remain plane breaks down. Occurs near point loads, supports, openings, and geometry changes. Also called a D-region; analysed using strut-and-tie models.

Steel bars or fabric embedded in concrete to carry tensile forces. In reinforced concrete design, concrete resists compression while reinforcement resists tension. Specified by bar diameter, grade (e.g. B500B), and layout.
Short for reinforcing bar. Deformed steel rods embedded in concrete to resist tensile and shear forces. Common grades include B500B (Eurocode) and Grade 60 (ASTM). Diameter ranges from 6 mm to 40 mm.
A thick concrete slab or block that sits on top of a group of piles and distributes the column load evenly between them.
The widened top section of a bridge pier that supports the bridge beams and distributes load into the pier.

A notched or recessed end of a precast concrete beam where it bears on its support. The notch allows the top of the beam to be flush with the support, but creates a stress concentration requiring reinforcement.

A short cantilever bracket projecting from a concrete or steel column to support a beam, precast element, or runway beam. Corbels are designed using strut-and-tie models and are governed by shear-friction behaviour.
A short concrete stub column above the foundation that raises a steel base plate above the floor level, keeping the steel clear of moisture and allowing grouting.

A steel plate or bar welded to the underside of a column base plate that projects into the concrete foundation. It transfers horizontal shear forces from the column into the foundation directly, rather than relying on friction alone.

A view of a structural member cut perpendicular to its length, revealing the shape and size of the section - e.g., I-shape, circular hollow, rectangular. The cross-section properties (area, second moment of area) determine how a member resists load.
Lowercase. Concrete with pre-tensioned or post-tensioned tendons.

The width of a crack in concrete, measured at the surface. Controlled by serviceability checks in Eurocode. Excessive crack widths can allow water ingress, cause corrosion of reinforcement, and indicate overstress.
The process of verifying that a structural element or connection satisfies all the relevant requirements of a design code. IDEA StatiCa automates code-checks using CBFEM analysis.
Lowercase. Warping of a cross-section. Less common term.

An eigenvalue analysis that determines the theoretical elastic critical load multiplier at which a structure becomes unstable. Also called LBA. Results quantify buckling risk but do not account for imperfections or material nonlinearity; higher-order analyses are needed for realistic assessment.

The process of verifying that a structure retains adequate load-bearing capacity and integrity during a fire. Approaches include prescriptive (tabulated data), simplified calculation, and advanced thermal-structural FEA per Eurocode EN 1993-1-2 (steel) or EN 1992-1-2 (concrete).

A verification that a structural member or connection can withstand a defined fire exposure (R30, R60, R90, etc.) without collapse. Considers reduced material yield strength and stiffness at elevated temperature.

Design of a structure to resist earthquake-induced inertial forces. Key concepts include ductility, energy dissipation, capacity design, and seismic action spectra per Eurocode EN 1998. Connections must remain ductile under reversed cyclic loading.

The maximum compressive force a structural element or soil can sustain in direct bearing before yielding, crushing, or punching through. In bolted connections, bearing capacity governs when the bolt presses against the plate hole edge.
Lowercase. Concrete contribution to stiffness between cracks.

The reduction in compressive strength of cracked reinforced concrete in the direction perpendicular to an existing crack. Tensile cracking in one direction reduces the concrete's ability to carry compression in another, and must be accounted for in non-linear FEA.
Lowercase. Visualization of load path through concrete.

A complete list of all reinforcement bars or structural components in a design, including diameter, length, quantity, bending shape, and total mass. Used for material procurement and workshop fabrication.
Lowercase. 'full report' used as a feature descriptor (bold on site).
Lowercase. Appears in bold on site as a descriptor, not a proper noun.
Concrete placed and cast in its final position on site, as opposed to precast concrete which is cast off-site. Cast-in-place construction allows complex shapes but requires formwork.
Lowercase. An anchor drilled/set after concrete has cured.

Short steel cylinders with a head welded to a steel beam to create composite action with a concrete slab poured over it. The head provides mechanical interlock that transfers shear between the steel and concrete.
Lowercase. Plain (non-ribbed) rebar, common in older structures (1970s-80s).
Lowercase. Prestressing tendons not bonded to surrounding concrete.
Lowercase. Tendons used for strengthening bridges and precast elements.

The resistance at the interface between an anchor (or rebar) and the surrounding concrete. Relies on adhesion, friction, and mechanical interlock. Critical for chemical anchors and reinforcement development lengths.

The region of a concrete member where a concentrated force - such as a prestressing tendon force or a post-installed anchor load - is introduced and dispersed into the surrounding concrete. Typically a D-region requiring special design.
Lowercase. A closed-loop reinforcement bar for shear resistance.
Lowercase. A steel strand or bar used in prestressing.
Lowercase. Computational method to find optimal reinforcement layout.

The distribution of internal stresses throughout a structural element. In FEA and CBFEM, the stress field is visualised as a colour map, showing where stresses are highest and where the material is close to its limit.

The arrangement and orientation of cracks in a concrete element under load. The crack pattern reveals the load path and tension trajectories - cracks form perpendicular to the principal tensile stress direction.
Lowercase. The ratio of demand to capacity, expressed as percentage.
PJP always all caps. Also 'PJP groove weld'. Introduced in v24.0.
An automated process in IDEA StatiCa that calculates the minimum required weld size for a connection to satisfy code requirements. Saves time compared to manual weld sizing iterations.
Two words, lowercase. Also called 'packing plate' in some contexts.
Elongated bolt holes that allow movement of a connected member parallel to the slot direction. Used to accommodate thermal expansion, construction tolerances, or deliberate sliding joints.
'WT' all caps. A structural tee cut from a wide-flange section.

Structural steel sections manufactured by cold-rolling or press-braking flat sheet steel at room temperature. Common shapes include C, Z, and sigma sections. Thinner than hot-rolled equivalents; governed by EN 1993-1-3.

A steel tube with a circular cross-section, specified by outer diameter and wall thickness (e.g. CHS 168.3x10). Efficient in compression and torsion; used as columns, bracing, and truss chords. Governed by EN 1993-1-1.
Lowercase. An angle piece used in connections. Also 'cleat manufacturing operation'.

Describes analysis or behaviour where the relationship between load and deformation is not proportional. Nonlinear analysis captures material yielding and geometric effects that linear analysis misses.
INCONSISTENCY: Some older support articles use 'non-linear' with hyphen.
Lowercase. Abbreviation: LTB. Note: some pages omit the hyphen.
Lowercase. Internal CBFEM solver feature for modeling member stiffness.
Lowercase. A method for incremental loading in Member.
Lowercase. Default setting from v22.0 requiring balanced loads.
Title case as a feature name. Selects the governing load combination.
Lowercase. A numerical issue in FEM analysis. 'Singularity check' and 'singularity warning'.

Assessment of a structure's resistance to failure under repeated cyclic loading. Fatigue cracks typically initiate at stress concentrations such as weld toes and grow under fluctuating stress ranges. Governed by EN 1993-1-9 (steel) using S-N curves and damage accumulation.
Capitalize when used as a category name: Stand-off, Direct, Mortar joint, Gap.

A layer of mortar between masonry units (bricks, blocks, or stones) that bonds them and transfers compressive and shear forces. Joint thickness, mortar strength, and detailing affect the load capacity and deformation behaviour of masonry walls.
Lowercase 'scene'. The 3D visualization window in the application.
Title case. A tab in the Connection application for defining loads.

term: Forces in Node, Forces in Bolts, Forces in Position
definition: Title case for each variation. Load input methods in Connection.
Capital C, lowercase s. A settings section in the application.
Capital C, lowercase t. Results display showing pass/fail checks.
Capitalize. The left-side panel for model navigation.
Title case both words. Used for parametric design advanced features.

American Institute of Steel Construction. The US body that produces the primary American steel design standard (AISC 360). AISC specifications are used throughout North America and internationally where US codes apply.
American Concrete Institute. The US body that produces ACI 318, the primary American concrete design standard. Widely used in North America and internationally.

European Norm (European Standard). The prefix used for Eurocodes - e.g. EN 1993 (steel), EN 1992 (concrete). 'EN' indicates the standard is adopted across all EU member states, replacing previous national codes.

AISC Seismic Provisions for Structural Steel Buildings. The US code governing the design of steel structures in seismic zones, covering special moment frames, concentrically braced frames, and other seismic systems.

AISC Prequalified Connections for Special and Intermediate Steel Moment Frames. Lists connection configurations that have been tested and pre-approved for seismic use - designers can use them without additional testing.

Building Code Requirements for Structural Concrete - the primary US code for reinforced concrete design. Covers beams, columns, slabs, foundations, and connections. Key design basis for concrete in North America.

[1st Generation Eurocode] Eurocode 3: Design of Steel Structures. The European standard covering hot-rolled sections, cold-formed sections, plated structures, and - critically for IDEA StatiCa - Part 1-8 covering the design of joints.

[1st Generation Eurocode] Eurocode 3, Part 1-8: Design of Joints. The 1st generation European standard for the design of steel connections - bolted, welded, and moment-resisting. Published in 2005 (with corrigendum AC:2009). The primary 1st generation code reference for steel connection design, and the basis on which IDEA StatiCa Connection was originally built.

Building Information Modelling. A digital process for creating and managing information about a building. In structural engineering, BIM models (from Tekla, Revit, etc.) are linked to IDEA StatiCa via Checkbot to extract connection geometry for design.

Finite Element Analysis. A computational method that divides a structure into small elements, calculates the behaviour of each, and assembles the results to find stresses, strains, and deformations throughout the whole structure.

Computer-Aided Design. Software used to create technical drawings and 3D models. In structural engineering, CAD tools (AutoCAD, Tekla, Revit) define the geometry that feeds into analysis and connection design.
Abbreviation for Application Programming Interface. Plural: APIs.

Representational State Transfer. An architectural style for building web APIs that communicate over HTTP using standard methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE). A REST API exposes data and actions as URLs (endpoints); clients send requests and receive responses, typically formatted as JSON. In the IDEA StatiCa context, the REST API allows external software (scripts, analysis tools, custom workflows) to create connection models, set loads, run calculations, and retrieve results programmatically - without opening the IDEA StatiCa user interface. Used by firms that want to automate repetitive connection checks or integrate IDEA StatiCa into their own design pipelines.

Compatible Stress Field Method - the analysis method used by IDEA StatiCa Detail for concrete D-regions. Computes stress fields in concrete consistent with the material's behaviour, satisfying both equilibrium and compatibility.

Materially Nonlinear Analysis. A finite element analysis that models material yielding and plastic behaviour while assuming geometry remains unchanged (small-displacement theory). Used in IDEA StatiCa to determine connection plastic resistance.

Ultimate Limit State - the design condition representing structural failure (collapse, fracture, instability). All structural elements must have sufficient resistance at ULS with appropriate safety factors applied to both loads and material strengths.

Serviceability Limit State - the design condition for normal use of the structure. Checks excessive deflection, vibration, cracking, and deformation that would impair the function or appearance of the structure, even if failure is not imminent.

Hollow Structural Section - the North American term for steel tubes with a hollow, closed cross-section. Can be circular (CHS), rectangular (RHS), or square (SHS). Very efficient for columns and members carrying both bending and torsion.
Abbreviation for Reinforced Concrete Section. Also an IDEA StatiCa module name.
Abbreviation for Industry Foundation Classes. Open BIM exchange format.
Abbreviation for Drawing Exchange Format. AutoCAD-origin file format.

The proprietary binary CAD file format native to AutoCAD, widely used for 2D and 3D structural drawings. Structural detailing offices exchange fabrication drawings in DWG format; most BIM and structural software can import it.
Abbreviation for Reduced Beam Section. A prequalified seismic connection type.

End Plate Moment connection. A bolted beam-to-column joint where a plate welded to the beam end is bolted to the column flange. Designed to transfer bending moment, shear, and axial force. Can be partial- or full-depth depending on the required moment resistance.

Welded Unreinforced Flange-Welded Web. A moment connection type prequalified under AISC 358 for use in Ordinary Moment Frames (OMF), Intermediate Moment Frames (IMF), and Special Moment Frames (SMF). The beam flanges are groove-welded to the column and the web is welded. All caps with hyphen.

Welded Unreinforced Flange-Bolted Web. A moment connection type prequalified under AISC 358 for use in Ordinary Moment Frames (OMF) only. The beam flanges are groove-welded to the column and the web is bolted. All caps with hyphen.
Abbreviation for Microsoft Word Open XML Document.
Abbreviation for Engineer of Record. Plural: EORs.
Abbreviation for Linear Buckling Analysis. A type of stability analysis for finding critical buckling modes.

Lateral-Torsional Buckling - a buckling mode affecting beams where the compression flange deflects laterally while the beam simultaneously twists. Prevented by providing lateral restraint to the compression flange (e.g. floor slab, purlins). Governed by EC3 Section 6.3.2.
Abbreviation for Geometrically and Materially Nonlinear Analysis. Like GMNIA but WITHOUT imperfections. Distinct from GMNIA.

Partial Joint Penetration - a butt weld that does not penetrate the full thickness of the connected material. Cheaper than full penetration but has lower capacity and cannot develop the full strength of the base metal. Used where the full joint strength is not required.
Abbreviation for Circular Hollow Section. Round tube steel section.
Abbreviation for Material and Product Range Library. The built-in material and cross-section database.
Abbreviation for European Technical Assessment. A European product approval document for construction products.
Abbreviation for International Code Council Evaluation Service. All caps with hyphen. US product evaluation/certification body.
Abbreviation for End User License Agreement. The software license agreement.
Abbreviation for Finite Element Method (or Model). Context-dependent: 'Method' (general) or 'Model' (specific). Distinct from FEA (Analysis).
Abbreviation for Local Coordinate System. The coordinate system relative to a member.
Abbreviation for Indian Standard for Steel. 'IS' all caps, space, number. Indian steel design standard.

Informal shorthand sometimes used for Hong Kong structural design codes, such as the 'Code of Practice for the Structural Use of Steel' (HKSS) or 'Code of Practice for Structural Use of Concrete' (HKCP), published by the Buildings Department of Hong Kong. Not a formally standardised abbreviation.
Abbreviation for Schweizerischer Ingenieur- und Architektenverein (Swiss code). All caps. Swiss engineering standards. E.g., SIA 262.
Abbreviation for Set of Rules (Russian). 'SP' all caps, space, number. Russian structural design standard.
Abbreviation for Guobiao (Chinese National Standard). 'GB' all caps. Chinese building code. Full format: GB50007-2011 (no spaces).

Abbreviation for Canadian Standards Association Steel Standard 2019. 'CSA' all caps, space, standard number, colon, year. Note: superseded by CSA S16:24 (published 2024), which is the current edition.

The 2022 edition of the AISC Specification for Structural Steel Buildings - the primary US standard governing the design of structural steel members and connections. Covers both LRFD (load and resistance factor design) and ASD (allowable strength design) methods.
Abbreviation for ACI 318, 2025 edition. Latest ACI concrete code.
Abbreviation for ACI 318, 2019 edition. Previous edition, still widely referenced.
Abbreviation for Australian Standard for Concrete. 'AS' all caps, space, number. Australian concrete standard.
Abbreviation for fib Model Code. Lowercase 'fib' (federation). 'Model Code' in title case. International concrete design reference.
Abbreviation for Austrian National Standard. Exact spelling with Ö umlaut.
Abbreviation for Shell elements in Beam/RCS. All caps. Shell elements for more realistic member modeling in Beam and RCS.

[2nd Generation Eurocode] A comprehensive revision of the original (1st generation) Eurocodes, developed by CEN/TC 250 from around 2015 onwards under European Commission Mandate M/515. First parts published in 2023 (EN 1990:2023). All 2nd generation parts must be published by 30 September 2027, with all conflicting 1st generation standards withdrawn by 30 March 2028.

[2nd Generation Eurocode] The 2nd generation Basis of Structural and Geotechnical Design - notably expanding scope to include geotechnical design alongside structural. Published 30 August 2023. Introduces a revised reliability framework, updated partial factors, clearer guidance on robustness and structural integrity, and improved rules for design assisted by testing. Forms the backbone of all other 2nd generation Eurocodes.

[2nd Generation Eurocode] The revised Eurocode 2 for concrete structures, currently in final stages of publication. Key changes include updated creep and shrinkage models, revised fire design rules, improved detailing rules for connections, and better integration with EN 1990:2023. Replaces EN 1992-1-1:2004 after national transition.

[2nd Generation Eurocode] The revised Eurocode 3 for steel structures. Key updates include higher strength steel grades (up to S700 incorporated directly into EN 1993-1-1), revised buckling curves, improved fatigue rules, and restructured parts. EN 1993-1-8:2024 (joints) introduces design-oriented finite element analysis as a formal code procedure - the category that CBFEM, as used by IDEA StatiCa, falls within.

[2nd Generation Eurocode] The published 2nd generation Eurocode 3 Part 1-8: Design of Joints (published 2024). Formally introduces design-oriented finite element analysis as a code procedure - which encompasses the CBFEM method used by IDEA StatiCa. Also harmonises National Annex parameters and reduces NDPs to improve cross-border consistency in connection design.

[2nd Generation Eurocode] The revised Eurocode 4 for composite steel-concrete structures, being updated in parallel with EN 1992 and EN 1993. Revised push-out test procedures, updated headed stud resistance models, and improved rules for composite connections are among the expected changes.

[2nd Generation Eurocode] A value or choice within a Eurocode that each country sets in its National Annex rather than the code itself. One of the goals of the 2nd generation Eurocodes is to significantly reduce the number of NDPs, making designs more consistent and comparable across EU member states.

[2nd Generation Eurocode] The coexistence window between 1st and 2nd generation Eurocodes. All conflicting 1st generation standards must be formally withdrawn by 30 March 2028, regardless of when a country adopts the 2nd generation version nationally. The length of coexistence therefore varies by part: EN 1990:2023 has roughly 4-5 years of coexistence; parts published closer to 2027 have a much shorter window.

American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials. The US body that publishes the primary design standards for highway bridges and transportation infrastructure. AASHTO specifications are adopted by US state Departments of Transportation (DOTs) and form the legal design basis for publicly funded bridge projects.

The primary US standard for highway bridge design, published by AASHTO. Uses Load and Resistance Factor Design (LRFD) - factored loads must not exceed factored resistance. Covers superstructures, substructures, foundations, and connections. Now in its 10th edition (2024). Mandatory on federally funded US bridge projects since 2007.

The AASHTO standard highway live load model, introduced in 1993. Consists of a design truck (72 kip / 320 kN gross weight), a design tandem (two 25 kip axles), and a lane load (0.64 kip/ft uniformly distributed). The critical effect of truck or tandem combined with lane load governs design. Used in all AASHTO LRFD bridge designs.

term: AASHTO Guide Spec for LRFD Seismic Bridge Design
definition: AASHTO's seismic design standard for highway bridges, providing an alternative to the seismic provisions in the main LRFD spec. Uses a displacement-based design philosophy. Classifies bridges into Seismic Design Categories (SDC A-D) based on site hazard. Emphasises ductile detailing of columns and connections to survive design earthquakes.

The original AASHTO bridge design code, based on Allowable Stress Design (ASD). Largely superseded by the LRFD specifications after the mandatory LRFD transition in 2007, but still used for some older bridge assessments and rehabilitation projects. Contrast with AASHTO LRFD, which uses factored load and resistance checks.

AASHTO LRFD defines specific load combinations for bridge design: Strength (I-V), Extreme Event (I-II for seismic/vessel collision), Service (I-IV for deflection/cracking), and Fatigue (I-II for stress range). Each combination uses different load factors. More complex than building codes due to the range of dynamic and vehicular effects.

The two dominant bridge and structural design code families worldwide. AASHTO governs in the US; Eurocodes govern in Europe and many other countries. Both use LRFD/limit state principles but differ in load models (HL-93 vs LM1), partial factors, material standards (ASTM vs EN), and connection design approaches. IDEA StatiCa supports both code families.

The IDEA StatiCa product family for reinforced concrete detail design. Two variants exist. Detail 2D uses the Compatible Stress Field Method (CSFM) to analyse discontinuity regions modelled as plane-stress problems - corbels, dapped ends, wall openings, pile caps, coupling beams, and similar 2D D-regions. Detail 3D extends analysis to three-dimensional problems where the geometry cannot be reduced to a single plane, with its primary validated use case being the design of steel-to-concrete connections: base plates, column pedestals, cast-in plates, anchors near edges, and shear lugs embedded in 3D concrete blocks. Both variants produce code-check reports to EN 1992 or ACI 318.

The analysis method used by IDEA StatiCa Detail. A plasticity-based approach that satisfies both equilibrium and compatibility simultaneously in reinforced concrete. More rigorous than strut-and-tie modelling because it accounts for the actual stress distribution and concrete softening due to transverse cracking.

A design method for D-regions that models the flow of forces through concrete as a truss: concrete carries compression (struts) and reinforcement carries tension (ties). Required by EN 1992 and ACI 318 for discontinuity regions. IDEA StatiCa Detail automates and verifies STM-type force flows using CSFM.

In strut-and-tie modelling, a concrete compression member representing the compressive stress field. Three types: prismatic (uniform cross-section), fan-shaped (spreading), and bottle-shaped (bulging). Strength is reduced from cylinder strength by an efficiency factor to account for cracking and biaxial stress states.

The tension member in a strut-and-tie model, normally a reinforcing bar or group of bars. The tie force equals the tension demand from the truss model. Anchorage of the tie beyond the nodal zone is critical - the bar must be fully developed by the point where the force is needed.

The region in a strut-and-tie model where struts and ties meet. Three types: CCC (all compression), CCT (one tie), CTT (two ties). The geometry and strength of the nodal zone control the achievable strut angle and anchor force, and must be checked for multi-directional compression.

A precast concrete beam with a notch cut into its end to reduce the overall structural depth at supports. Creates a complex D-region with multiple potential failure planes. Requires careful reinforcement detailing at the re-entrant corner to prevent diagonal cracking. Commonly analysed in IDEA StatiCa Detail.

A beam sufficiently deep that conventional beam theory (plane sections remain plane) does not apply across its full depth. Under EN 1992-1-1 clause 5.3.1(3), a beam is classified as deep when its effective span is less than 3 times its overall depth (l < 3h). Under ACI 318 Section 9.9.1.1, a deep beam has a clear span not exceeding 4 times the overall depth, or concentrated loads within 2h of the support face. The entire member is a D-region; shear is carried by direct arch action and design must use STM or CSFM rather than standard beam shear equations.

A heavily loaded beam that collects loads from columns or walls above and transfers them to columns or walls below, often spanning across an opening in the structure. Almost always a deep beam D-region with complex load paths. Common in podium structures and carparks.

A bridge pier with a wide, flat cap beam resembling a hammer head in cross-section. The cap beam is a D-region subject to high shear and torsion from eccentric loading. Requires STM or detailed FEA for design. Common in highway bridge and viaduct design.

A short, deep beam connecting adjacent structural walls at each floor level. Allows the walls to act as a coupled shear wall system with significantly increased lateral stiffness and energy dissipation. High shear demand means standard beam shear design may not apply - often requires diagonal reinforcement.

Reinforcement provided around openings in concrete walls or slabs to replace the interrupted reinforcement and control crack widths. Typically diagonal bars at corners to redirect force flow around the opening, plus trimmer bars. The region around the opening is a D-region best analysed with STM or CSFM.

A failure mode in flat slabs and pad footings where a column or pile punches through the slab along a truncated cone surface. Checked on a defined control perimeter. Critical in flat plate construction. EN 1992 and ACI 318 provide design equations; IDEA StatiCa Detail can model the punching region explicitly.

The minimum length of reinforcing bar that must be embedded in concrete to transfer the full yield force from the bar to the surrounding concrete through bond. Depends on bar diameter, concrete strength, cover, confinement, and coating. Must be satisfied at all cut-off points and at nodal zones in STM.

Tensile stresses that develop in concrete perpendicular to a compression strut or anchor tension force, caused by the spreading of a concentrated force. Can cause longitudinal splitting cracks. Controlled by confinement reinforcement (links or hoops) and by keeping stress levels below cracking limits. Critical in anchor design and near supports.

A beam with a ledge or nib projecting from its side to support the end of a secondary beam or precast plank without the secondary member sitting on top. The ledge and its connection to the main beam form a D-region requiring careful detailing of the hanger reinforcement and the local bearing.

The engineer responsible for the detailed design of structural connections, specifying weld sizes, bolt grades and patterns, plate thicknesses, and checking all failure modes against the design code. IDEA StatiCa Connection is the primary calculation tool; IDEA StatiCa Checkbot is used to manage and batch-check every connection across the full project model. Connection design may be carried out by the fabricator's engineer, a specialist consultant, or the EOR.

A draughtsperson or technician who produces the detailed fabrication and erection drawings from the engineer's design. In steelwork, the detailer works within the fabricator's team and interprets connection designs into full shop drawings. Increasingly uses 3D BIM software (Tekla, Revit, SDS/2) and exports models directly to IDEA StatiCa via the BIM link or Checkbot. The IDEA StatiCa Viewer allows the detailer to review the engineer's connection model and results without a full licence.

The company that manufactures structural steelwork in a workshop: cutting, drilling, welding, and priming members and connections to the engineer's drawings. The fabricator's team often carries out delegated connection design using IDEA StatiCa Connection and manages project-wide checks via Checkbot. In Europe, fabricators must hold CE Marking under EN 1090-1 (using EN 1090-2 as the execution standard for workmanship and tolerances) and design connections to EN 1993-1-8. In the US, fabricators follow AISC 303 (Code of Standard Practice), AWS D1.1 (Structural Welding Code), RCSC (bolt tightening), and AISC 360 for connection resistance; AISC Certification is the equivalent quality mark. IDEA StatiCa Connection supports both code regimes in the same software.

The licensed structural engineer who takes overall responsibility for the structural design of a project. Signs and seals the structural drawings. In delegated design, the EOR defines the design loads and performance requirements for connections but may allow the fabricator or specialist to size them, subject to the EOR's review and approval.

An arrangement, common in North America and increasingly in the UK, where the EOR specifies the design forces for each connection and delegates the detailed design to the steel fabricator or their specialist engineer. The fabricator uses IDEA StatiCa or tables to design each connection and submits calculations for the EOR's review.

The engineer who builds and runs the global structural model (typically in Robot, SAP2000, ETABS, or similar) to determine member forces and reactions throughout the structure. Their output - beam end forces, column loads, reaction envelopes - forms the input to IDEA StatiCa for connection and detail design.

An engineer specialising in detailed FEA of complex components or regions using general-purpose solvers such as ANSYS, ABAQUS, or LS-DYNA, or specialist structural tools. In the IDEA StatiCa context, CBFEM is the built-in FEA engine; a standalone FEA specialist is typically engaged only for unusually complex or novel connection geometries.

An engineer - separate from the designer - who reviews calculations, drawings, and models to confirm the design is correct and code-compliant. In the UK, the Building Safety Act 2022 introduced mandatory independent structural assessment for higher-risk buildings (broadly, residential buildings of 18 m or 7 storeys or more); for other buildings it is strong professional practice and often required by clients and insurers, but not universally mandated by law. IDEA StatiCa Checkbot provides a project-wide dashboard of connection check statuses, making it straightforward for a checker to review and sign off each connection. The free IDEA StatiCa Viewer allows reviewers to inspect results without a full licence.

The team member responsible for managing the 3D digital model and ensuring consistency between disciplines (architecture, structure, MEP). For steelwork, the BIM coordinator oversees the Tekla or Revit model from which IDEA StatiCa Connection imports geometry directly via the BIM link. IDEA StatiCa Checkbot sits between the BIM model and IDEA StatiCa, providing a connection management layer: all joints are listed, their check status is visible, and the coordinator can track which connections have been designed and approved.

The specialist steelwork contractor responsible for assembling and connecting the prefabricated steel frame on site. Distinct from the fabricator. The erector follows the erection procedure and uses the connection design (bolted site joints, temporary connections) to assemble the structure safely in sequence.

The company that casts, cures, stresses (if prestressed), and delivers precast concrete elements. Responsible for production quality, dimensional tolerances, and handling documentation (including lifting and transport load calculations). Often uses IDEA StatiCa Detail to design connection zones, corbels, and dapped ends within their precast elements.

A procurement route in which a single entity holds contracts for both design and construction. The contractor employs or engages the structural engineer and the fabricator. This arrangement increases the contractor's control over connection and detail design decisions, and tools like IDEA StatiCa add value by reducing design-fabrication iteration time.

A structural concrete component - beam, column, slab, wall panel, or staircase - cast in a factory under controlled conditions and transported to site for erection. Factory production improves quality and speed but introduces additional load cases: demoulding, storage, transport, and erection, each of which may govern the reinforcement design.

A precast beam in which high-tensile tendons (wires or strands) are pre-tensioned before casting or post-tensioned after. The prestress introduces a permanent compression force that counteracts tensile bending stresses under service loads, allowing longer spans and shallower depths than conventionally reinforced beams. Typical sections: I, inverted T, U, Super T, Y-beam.

The structural load case representing forces on a precast element during road or rail transport. Typically modelled as a simply supported beam on two support points (dunnage positions) subject to self-weight amplified by a dynamic factor. May govern tension in the top flange of an inverted-T or I-beam, requiring additional top steel.

A multiplier applied to static self-weight to account for road surface irregularities and vibration during transport. Commonly 1.3 to 2.0 depending on road quality, element length, and support conditions. Specified in transport standards (e.g. UK BD 86 for abnormal loads) or agreed with the transport engineer.

Timber or rubber packing materials placed between a precast element and the truck bed or between stacked elements in storage, at specified positions to support the element without inducing unwanted bending. Dunnage position is critical: supports must be at the designed lifting/support points, not randomly placed.

The designated location on a precast element where lifting inserts (loops, anchors, or ferrules) are cast in to allow the element to be lifted by crane. For a uniformly loaded element on two symmetric pick points, the optimal position that equalises the hogging moment at the inserts with the mid-span sagging moment is approximately 0.207L from each end - not the quarter-points. Quarter-point lifting leaves the mid-span moment unnecessarily high. For elements with sections weakened by notches or openings, the lift point positions must be adapted to avoid overstress at those locations.

A cast-in steel device - loop, ferrule, anchor plate, or proprietary clutch insert - embedded in a precast element to accept lifting equipment. Designed for the full lift force including dynamic effects. Must be checked for concrete cone pullout, edge effects, and group interaction in accordance with EN 1992-4 or equivalent anchoring design code.

The upward precamber deliberately induced in a prestressed beam by the eccentric prestress force. Camber is intended to offset the anticipated sagging deflection under dead and live loads. Because camber varies with time (creep) and production tolerances, it must be managed during erection and in the floor level design.

Lateral bow of a precast element, measured as the maximum offset from a straight line between the two ends. Arises from casting inaccuracies, differential shrinkage, and eccentric prestress. Excessive sweep can cause difficulties during erection and may affect lateral stability of slender beams during transport and before permanent bracing is in place.

The check that a slender precast beam will not overturn or fail in lateral bending when transported on a truck. A beam lying on its side is much weaker than when upright. Critical parameters are the beam's lateral bending stiffness, the height of the support points, the lateral stiffness of the truck, and the dynamic transverse acceleration.

The planned order in which structural elements are lifted and connected on site, designed to maintain stability of the partially built structure at every stage. For precast concrete, the erection sequence must ensure that temporary propping, bracing, and grouting operations are completed before the next elements are placed.

Temporary steel or timber props used to support precast or in-situ concrete elements until joints are grouted, in-situ concrete has gained strength, or the permanent structure is complete. Props must be designed for their loads and have a clear removal procedure - premature removal before strength is achieved is a common cause of collapse.

A flexible elastomeric (rubber or neoprene) or hard (steel, PTFE) pad placed between a precast element and its support. Accommodates relative rotation and differential settlement, distributes bearing stress, and prevents hard point contact which could cause edge spalling. Pad dimensions govern the local bearing pressure and the required seat width.

The minimum length of bearing required at the end of a precast element to ensure it cannot fall off its support under worst-case movements. Accounts for manufacturing tolerances, setting-out tolerances, thermal movement, and seismic displacement. Governed by EN 1992-1-1 Section 10 for precast or AASHTO LRFD for bridges.

The stress induced in a precast element during demoulding, lifting, transport, or erection - typically before the full design strength of the concrete has been achieved and before any composite action with a topping slab. Handling stresses often govern the design of the top flange reinforcement in prestressed beams and the skin reinforcement in slender panels.

A precast connection where projecting reinforcement from one element passes through a pocket or sleeve cast into the adjacent element, which is then filled with non-shrink grout. Transfers tension, compression, and shear. The pocket provides tolerance during erection, and the grouted bar must achieve full development within the pocket depth.

An anchor failure mode in which the anchor pulls out of the concrete while the surrounding concrete remains intact - the anchor displaces relative to the concrete rather than the concrete fracturing as a cone. Occurs in smooth bars or anchors with insufficient bearing area at their tip. Prevented by using headed anchors, bent bars, or adequate embedment.

A concrete failure mode for anchors loaded in shear, particularly short, stiff anchors where the anchor tries to rotate and pry out a concrete mass on the side opposite to the load direction. Under ACI 318-19 Section 17.7.3, pryout capacity is 1.0 times the concrete breakout capacity in tension for anchors with hef < 63.5 mm, or 2.0 times for hef >= 63.5 mm. Under EN 1992-4, the pryout coefficient is fixed at k = 2.0 regardless of embedment depth. Governs for short, stiff anchors with low embedment-to-diameter ratios.

A tension failure mode in anchor design where a cone of concrete is pulled out of the base material. The projected area method (used in EN 1992-4 and ACI 318 Ch.17) calculates capacity from the projected area of the failure cone on the concrete surface, modified for edge distance, spacing, and eccentricity. Critical design check for all tension anchors.

The distance from the centreline of an anchor to the nearest free edge of the concrete. A small edge distance reduces concrete breakout and splitting capacity significantly. EN 1992-4 defines minimum edge distances to avoid splitting during installation and specifies how edge distance modifies the characteristic breakout resistance. Critical for anchors near slab edges, beam ends, and wall faces.

The effective depth to which an anchor is embedded in concrete, measured from the concrete surface to the load-bearing element (nut, head, or bond end). Governs concrete cone breakout capacity, bond capacity (adhesive anchors), and pullout capacity. Increasing embedment depth is the most effective way to improve anchor tension resistance.

The reduction in breakout resistance when multiple anchors are spaced closely enough that their failure cones overlap. The group is less efficient than the sum of individual anchor capacities. EN 1992-4 accounts for this using the ratio of actual projected breakout area to theoretical non-overlapping area. Anchors beyond a critical spacing (typically 3 times the embedment depth) are treated independently.

Reinforcement in the vicinity of an anchor that can intercept potential breakout failure surfaces. In EN 1992-4, supplementary reinforcement provides a modest benefit by allowing a higher partial factor, but does not need to carry the full load by itself. In ACI 318, the equivalent concept is 'anchor reinforcement' (Section 17.5.2) - a more demanding approach where the reinforcement must be specifically designed and detailed to transfer the full design load across the failure surface, completely replacing the concrete breakout check rather than supplementing it. The two approaches are not equivalent and must not be confused.

The anchor resistance value corresponding to a defined fractile of the statistical distribution of test results, typically the 5th percentile. Determined from product approval testing (ETA in Europe; ICC-ES report in the US) under controlled conditions. Used with partial safety factors to calculate the design resistance for comparison with design actions.

The document granting CE Marking to a post-installed anchor product for use in Europe. Issued by an approved Technical Assessment Body (TAB) on the basis of a European Assessment Document (EAD) - the current framework under Construction Products Regulation EU 305/2011. Contains the characteristic resistances for all relevant failure modes across approved concrete strength classes and installation conditions. Required for use of post-installed anchors under EN 1992-4. Earlier ETAs were issued against ETAGs (European Technical Approval Guidelines), which have since been replaced by EADs.

The design assumption that concrete in the tension zone has cracked, reducing the bearing resistance of anchors. EN 1992-4 and ACI 318 require the engineer to justify whether uncracked conditions can be guaranteed; if not, the lower cracked-concrete resistance values must be used. Post-installed anchors must be tested and approved separately for cracked and uncracked conditions.

A layer of non-shrink cementitious or epoxy grout placed between the underside of a steel baseplate and the concrete foundation to provide full contact, accommodate level tolerances, and transfer compressive forces uniformly. Typically 25 to 75 mm thick. The grout must be considered in the anchor design because it affects the effective embedment depth and lever arm for shear.

The additional requirements for anchors in seismic design categories C through F (ACI 318 Section 17.10) or seismic design situations (EN 1992-4). ACI 318 provides three compliance routes: (a) ductile steel failure governs over all concrete failure modes; (b) the attached structure or element is designed to remain elastic under seismic loads; or (c) a 0.4 reduction factor is applied to the concrete breakout capacity. Seismically tested and approved anchors with demonstrated ductile cyclic performance are often required, particularly in high seismic risk categories.

Informal name for SCI/BCSA publication P358 'Joints in Steel Construction: Simple Joints to Eurocode 3'. Provides standardised design tables for common simple connections used in the UK: fin plates, flexible end plates, and web cleat connections. Double angle web cleats are not covered in P358 (they were included in the predecessor P212 but omitted from P358 as they are no longer commonly used in modern UK practice). The tables give bolt numbers, weld sizes, and component dimensions for given shear and tying forces, eliminating the need for individual calculation.

Informal name for SCI publication P363 'Steel Building Design: Design Data'. Contains section property tables, buckling curves, and resistance tables for standard UK hot-rolled steel sections to Eurocode 3. Used by connection designers to look up section properties needed for connection calculations and by detailers to specify sections.

A connection designed to transfer bending moment between members, providing rotational continuity. EN 1993-1-8 uses two independent classification systems: by stiffness (rigid, semi-rigid, or nominally pinned) and by strength (full-strength, partial-strength, or nominally pinned). A rigid connection has stiffness above the code threshold; a full-strength connection has moment capacity at least equal to the connected member. These are separate properties - a connection can be rigid but partial-strength. Moment connections typically use extended end plates, haunched connections, or directly welded flanges.

A simple shear connection where a plate is shop-welded to part of the depth of the supported beam web (not the full height) and site-bolted to the supporting member's flange or web. Also called a partial depth end plate. The plate is thin and short enough to flex and release moment under load. Distinguished from the full-depth end plate, which extends to both flanges and is a separate connection type. Covered in Green Book P358.

A moment connection where the end plate extends beyond the beam top and/or bottom flange, allowing additional bolt rows above and below the flanges to resist the applied moment as a bolt force couple. The bolts in the tension zone are the critical design component. Classified as rigid or partial-strength depending on plate stiffness, bolt stiffness, and flange flexibility.

A connection joining two lengths of column, typically at mid-height between floors to simplify erection. Must transfer compression, bending, shear, and tying forces. In pure compression splices, the load may be transferred by direct bearing between machined surfaces (bearing splice); tension cases require bolted cover plates or end-plate connections.

A connection joining two lengths of beam in the span. Must transfer moment, shear, and axial force at the splice location. Splice position is chosen to minimise design forces, often near a point of contraflexure. May use bolted cover plates to flanges and webs, or welded joints. Temporary stability during erection is a key design consideration.

A moment connection to a column in which the beam is deepened at the connection by welding a triangular haunch below the bottom flange. The haunch increases the lever arm for the bolt group or weld, reducing bolt forces for a given moment. Common in portal frames. The haunch geometry is set by the moment demand and the practical constraints of the bolt pitch.

A bolted moment connection used for circular hollow section (CHS) members, particularly wind turbine towers, monopoles, and pipelines. A thick forged or welded ring flange is site-bolted to a matching ring on the adjacent member. Design must account for prying action of the circular flange plate and the non-uniform bolt force distribution around the ring.
