A connection involving circular (CHS) or rectangular (RHS/SHS) hollow sections. Behaviour is dominated by local deformation of the chord face. Classified by joint type: T, Y, K, N, X. Design in Eurocode 3 Part 1-8 uses dimensionless parameters (beta, gamma, eta) to determine the governing failure mode (chord face yielding, punching shear, shear yielding of chord).

A plate shop-welded to the web of a column within the connection panel zone to increase its shear strength and stiffness. Used where the panel zone shear demand from beam flanges in a moment connection exceeds the web's capacity without reinforcement. The doubler plate must be fully welded to transfer the additional shear force.

A horizontal stiffener plate welded to the column web and flanges at the beam flange level in a moment connection. Also called a transverse stiffener or column flange stiffener. Its purpose is to prevent local flange bending and web buckling at the point of concentrated force from the beam flange. Required when the column web and flanges are too thin to resist the flange force alone. Note: 'through plate' is a different component used in hollow section connections and should not be confused with a continuity plate.

A short angle section bolted or welded to a column or beam to provide a temporary seating for a secondary beam during erection, before permanent bolts are tightened. The cleat carries a small proportion of the final shear; the web connection carries the majority. Also used as a permanent bearing connection in some secondary framing situations.

A minimum horizontal tensile force that all connections in a building structure must be able to resist to provide robustness and prevent progressive collapse following an accidental event. Required by EN 1991-1-7 and structural integrity clauses of national building codes. The tying force is distinct from the design shear and must be checked as an additional ULS combination.

The rotational stiffness of a connection, relating the applied bending moment to the resulting rotation. EN 1993-1-8 classifies connections as rigid (stiffness above upper bound), semi-rigid (between bounds), or pinned (below lower bound). The stiffness must be consistent with the assumptions made in the global analysis model. IDEA StatiCa Connection calculates and reports connection stiffness.

A steel plate welded to the foot of a steel column to distribute the column load to the concrete foundation. Must be designed for compression (bearing), tension (anchor bolts), and shear (friction or shear lug). Base plate thickness is governed by bending of the plate cantilever beyond the column flange or web. Critical in portal frame design and seismic applications.

A small cutout in the web of a steel member at the flange-to-web junction, providing access for the welder to deposit a full-penetration groove weld across the full flange width. Shape and dimensions are specified in standards (AWS D1.1, AISC) as the profile affects fatigue performance. Seismically critical connections require carefully profiled holes to avoid stress concentrations.

A conservative set of standardised connection forces applied uniformly across all connections of a given type when actual connection forces from the global analysis are unavailable or the analysis is at an early stage. Commonly used in design-and-build projects where connections are sized before the final global model is complete. IDEA StatiCa can batch-check connections against blanket force sets.

The worst-case combination of forces at a given location across all load combinations and load patterns. For a connection this may be, for example, the maximum shear combined with the maximum tension, or the maximum moment with minimum axial. IDEA StatiCa allows multiple load cases to be imported and checked; the envelope defines the governing combination for each failure mode.

A table or matrix of the critical force combinations that a connection or element must be designed to resist, derived by scanning all load combinations and extracting the governing set for each failure mode. May include maximum positive and negative values of each force component, and the forces co-existing with each maximum. Used as input to IDEA StatiCa Connection.

An equivalent horizontal force applied to the structure in the global analysis to account for initial out-of-plumb geometric imperfections. EN 1993-1-1 Clause 5.3.2 defines the basic sway imperfection as phi_0 = 1/200 (0.5%), but the actual applied force is reduced by height factor alpha_h and column-number factor alpha_m - so in practice the applied force is typically less than 0.5% of the vertical design load. The 0.5% value is the base (maximum) value before reductions, not a minimum. Generates lateral connection forces that would otherwise be zero in a perfectly upright frame.

A load that reduces a beam's resistance to lateral-torsional buckling because it is applied above the shear centre - typically to the top flange. As the beam buckles laterally, the load shifts to increase the overturning tendency. Under EN 1993-1-1, the effect is accounted for by a lower elastic critical moment Mcr (computed with the load application point above the shear centre), which raises the non-dimensional slenderness and reduces the buckling resistance factor. A stabilising load applied at or below the shear centre has the opposite effect, increasing Mcr.

The tensile membrane action that develops in a beam when it has undergone large deflections following loss of a support or severe loading. The beam acts like a cable, carrying load predominantly in tension. EN 1991-1-7 and UFC 4-023-03 require that connections have sufficient tying capacity and deformation to develop catenary action as an alternate load path.

The ability of a structure to withstand an accidental event (explosion, vehicle impact, fire) without disproportionate collapse. Achieved by providing alternate load paths, tying connections together, and ensuring connections can deform without fracture. Governed by EN 1991-1-7 Annex A/B and UFC 4-023-03 in the US. Connection ductility and tying capacity are critical design parameters.

A load combination in EN 1990 that combines the permanent loads, a reduced variable load, and an accidental action (fire, explosion, vehicle impact) with reduced partial safety factors. Used to check structural integrity and robustness. The reduced factors reflect the low probability that maximum variable loads coincide with an accidental event.

The flagship IDEA StatiCa product for steel connection design and code-checking using CBFEM. Engineers model the connection geometry, apply loads, run analysis, and receive a complete code-check report to EN 1993, AISC 360, or other supported codes. The product integrates with Tekla, Revit, Robot, SAP2000, ETABS, and other CAD/analysis software via direct BIM links.

An IDEA StatiCa product that analyses individual steel members - beams, columns, or frames - including cross-section checks and lateral-torsional buckling, using MNA and GMNIA. Handles tapered members, haunched rafters, and non-standard cross-sections that are difficult to check with standard code tables. Provides code-check primarily to EN 1993-1-1 and EN 1993-1-5 (plate buckling). EN 1993-1-3 (cold-formed sections) checks are not automatically performed; users must apply those verifications manually for thin-walled sections outside the scope of EN 1993-1-1.

An IDEA StatiCa product for reinforced concrete cross-section design and code-checking. Checks beams, columns, and walls under combined bending, shear, torsion, and axial force. Generates interaction diagrams and capacity envelopes. Used by RC frame designers as an alternative to general-purpose analysis software for detailed section checks to EN 1992.

The process within IDEA StatiCa of comparing calculated stresses, strains, bolt forces, and weld throat utilisation against code-defined limits. Reported as a utilisation ratio (demand divided by capacity) for every component. The connection passes when all utilisation ratios are below 1.0 (100%). Components at or above the limit are highlighted red in the graphical output.

The component-based steps in IDEA StatiCa Connection that build up the connection model: adding members, plates (end plates, stiffeners, gusset plates, base plates, cleats, splice plates), cuts and offsets, wideners, and fasteners (welds and bolts). Each operation modifies the FE mesh and the resulting stress distribution. The order of operations determines the correct geometry and matters for accurate FE model generation. The operations correspond to real fabrication steps, helping engineers and detailers verify that the connection is constructable.

The automated classification of a connection as rigid, semi-rigid, or nominally pinned, based on the computed initial rotational stiffness compared to the thresholds in EN 1993-1-8 Figure 5.4. IDEA StatiCa Connection reports the initial stiffness after the CBFEM analysis, allowing the engineer to verify that the connection stiffness is consistent with the global analysis assumptions.

An analysis that accounts for material yielding but assumes the structure remains geometrically linear (small deformations). The stiffness matrix is updated as elements yield. Used in IDEA StatiCa Member for cross-section and member resistance checks. Captures plastic redistribution within a cross-section and member without the complexity of geometric non-linearity.

term: GMNIA (Geometric and Material Non-linear Analysis with Imperfections)
definition: The most rigorous analysis type in EN 1993-1-1, combining geometric non-linearity (both P-Delta global sway effects and P-delta local bow effects), material non-linearity (yielding), and initial geometric imperfections in a single model. Used in IDEA StatiCa Member to directly determine buckling resistance of complex steel members such as tapered rafters and haunched members. When correctly applied with appropriate imperfection amplitudes and boundary conditions, GMNIA eliminates the need for separate buckling reduction factors (chi).

The direct software interface between IDEA StatiCa and a structural analysis or detailing program. Supported links include Tekla Structures, Autodesk Revit, SCIA Engineer, Robot Structural Analysis, SAP2000, ETABS, Advance Steel, and others. The link passes connection geometry, member forces, and load cases from the host program to IDEA StatiCa, and can write results back, eliminating manual data re-entry.

A check in IDEA StatiCa Connection that evaluates the connection's overall resistance, rotational stiffness, and deformation (rotation) capacity based on the CBFEM analysis results, verifying compliance with the ductility and rotation requirements of EN 1993-1-8. Ensures the connection meets the stiffness classification it was assumed to have in the global analysis - rigid, semi-rigid, or nominally pinned. Particularly relevant for simple connections, which must demonstrate adequate rotation capacity to redistribute moments without fracture.

In IDEA StatiCa Connection, the maximum allowable equivalent plastic strain in a steel plate used as the CBFEM material failure criterion. Typically limited to 5% in the IDEA StatiCa CBFEM methodology, a limit established through calibration against physical tests and validation studies - not a direct clause in EN 1993. Plastic strain concentration at re-entrant corners, weld toes, and bolt holes indicates local overstress; elements exceeding the limit are highlighted red in the results view.

The dependence of FEA results on the size and type of the finite element mesh. In CBFEM, IDEA StatiCa uses a predefined meshing strategy that has been validated against tests and hand calculations. Users should not manually coarsen the mesh. Results should be checked for mesh sensitivity when modelling unusual geometries by refining and comparing.

The process of bringing member end forces (N, Vy, Vz, Mx, My, Mz) from a global analysis model into IDEA StatiCa via a BIM link or manual entry. Multiple load cases can be imported and checked simultaneously. The governing (worst) utilisation across all load cases is reported. Correct sign convention and member orientation must be verified after import.

The ratio of the peak local stress at a geometric discontinuity (notch, hole, change in cross-section) to the nominal stress remote from the discontinuity. High Kt values at weld toes, bolt holes, and re-entrant corners drive fatigue crack initiation. Controlled by good detailing: smooth transitions, avoiding sharp corners, grinding weld toes in fatigue-critical joints.

The branch of mechanics dealing with the behaviour of materials containing cracks. Applied to structural steel to determine critical crack sizes, stress intensity factors, and conditions for brittle fracture. Underpins Charpy impact testing requirements and the selection of steel sub-grades for low-temperature or thick-plate applications in welded connections.

The shear demand in the column web within the beam-column connection panel zone, generated by the opposing beam flange forces in a moment connection. If the panel zone is inadequate, it will yield in shear before the beam or column reaches its capacity. Checked under EN 1993-1-8 Section 6.2.6 and AISC 360 Section J10.6 (Web Panel Zone Shear). Resistance is provided by the column web alone or supplemented with a doubler plate or supplementary web plate.

A structural member with a cross-section that varies along its length, typically by varying the web depth or flange width. Common in portal frame rafters and eaves haunch regions to match the bending moment diagram and reduce material use. Standard code buckling checks do not directly apply; GMNIA in IDEA StatiCa Member or specialist software is required.

A deepened section at the eaves of a portal frame, created by welding a tapered rafter offcut below the bottom flange of the rafter at its junction with the column. Transfers the large eaves bending moment efficiently and provides the geometry for the eaves moment connection. As a rule of thumb for initial sizing, the haunch length is often taken as approximately 10% of the span; the actual length and depth are set by the bending moment diagram and the required connection lever arm, and must be verified in design.

The ridge connection of a portal frame where two rafters meet. Transfers relatively modest bending moments (the apex is typically near the point of contraflexure), shear, and axial force. The standard arrangement is two rafter end plates bolted face-to-face, sometimes with additional bolt rows in an extended plate configuration if the apex moment is significant. Often the least demanding connection in the portal frame to design.

A beam, typically a heavy plate girder or standard section with a rail on top, designed to carry the wheel loads from an overhead travelling crane. Subject to repeated, fatigue-inducing loads. Connection design is critical: the top flange must be detailed to avoid fatigue cracking at the connection point, and the end connections must transfer large cyclic horizontal (surge) forces.

Non-shrink cementitious or epoxy grout packed beneath a steel base plate after column erection to ensure full bearing contact with the concrete foundation. Must achieve specified compressive strength before loads are applied. Grout thickness is typically 25-50 mm; the grout layer affects the effective embedment of anchor bolts and must be included in the anchor design model.

The complete assembly of anchor bolt, nut, washer, and often a sleeve or oversized hole in the base plate that allows adjustment during erection. The oversized hole is later filled with grout. Bolt projection above the base plate must accommodate the grout thickness, nut, washer, and allowance for error, typically 100-150 mm above the finished concrete level.

A seismic design philosophy in which the structure is detailed to ensure that energy dissipation occurs in designated ductile zones (plastic hinges) while all other components - including connections - are designed with sufficient overstrength to remain elastic. Connections in a capacity-designed structure must be stronger than the member they connect, not just able to resist the design forces.

Collapse of a structure to an extent disproportionate to the initiating cause. Avoided by ensuring that the failure of a single element does not lead to the loss of a large floor or wall area. Regulated in EN 1991-1-7 and in UK Building Regulations Part A. Key measures include tying connections, protected key elements, and adequate robustness.

Permitted deviations from the specified geometry in fabrication and erection of steelwork. EN 1090-2 Annex C specifies essential tolerances (the minimum mandatory set for all structures, covering both fabrication and erection), and Annex D specifies functional tolerances (additional tolerances for specific structural or fit-up requirements). Connection design must accommodate these tolerances: oversized or slotted holes, adjustable base plates, and site-welded connections all address tolerance management.

The European standard 'Execution of steel structures and aluminium structures - Part 2: Technical requirements for steel structures'. Specifies fabrication tolerances, welding procedures, bolt tightening methods, and quality management requirements. CE Marking of structural steelwork requires compliance with EN 1090-2. Defines four Execution Classes (EXC1-4) with increasing quality requirements.

A classification system in EN 1090-2 that defines the level of quality requirements for fabricating and erecting steel structures. EXC1 is the least demanding (simple, low-consequence structures); EXC4 is the most demanding (nuclear, special). The Execution Class affects requirements for welder qualification, NDT inspection, documentation, and traceability. Selected by the designer based on consequence class and usage.

Inspection methods that evaluate the integrity of welds and materials without damaging the component. Includes visual inspection (VT), ultrasonic testing (UT), magnetic particle inspection (MPI), dye penetrant inspection (DPI), and radiographic testing (RT). Required extents and methods are specified in EN 1090-2 based on Execution Class and weld type. Critical for quality assurance in welded connections.

A document specifying the parameters (process, filler material, joint geometry, preheat, heat input, post-weld heat treatment) to be used for a particular weld. The WPS must be qualified by a Weld Procedure Qualification Record (WPQR) based on destructive testing of test welds. EN 1090-2 requires qualified WPS for EXC2, EXC3, and EXC4. Multiple qualification standards are accepted: EN ISO 15614-1 is the most common, but EN ISO 15610, 15611, 15612, and 15613 are also permitted depending on the welding process and application.

A free IDEA StatiCa application that acts as a connection management hub between structural analysis or BIM software and IDEA StatiCa Connection. It lists every joint in the imported model and shows a summary check status (not checked, passed, failed) for each. Users can open any connection directly in IDEA StatiCa Connection for full design and result review - which requires an IDEA StatiCa Connection licence. The free element is the Checkbot hub and status overview; detailed CBFEM result inspection still requires a licence. Used by connection designers, fabricators, BIM coordinators, and checkers/EOR to track and manage connection design progress across a project.

The plane-stress mode of IDEA StatiCa Detail. Models a reinforced concrete discontinuity region as a 2D cross-section in the plane of the applied forces, using CSFM. Suitable for corbels, dapped end beams, deep beams, wall openings, standard pile caps, and any D-region where the structure and loading can be represented in a single plane. Faster to set up than 3D and directly applicable to the majority of everyday concrete detail design tasks. Outputs include principal stress flows, reinforcement utilisations, and a code-check report to EN 1992 or ACI 318.

The three-dimensional mode of IDEA StatiCa Detail. Its primary validated and commercially released use case is the design of steel-to-concrete connections where the concrete block must be modelled in 3D: anchor groups near multiple edges, base plates on 3D column pedestals, cast-in plates, and shear lugs where 2D simplification would be inaccurate. Uses CSFM in 3D solid elements to determine concrete stresses, reinforcement utilisations, and anchor forces simultaneously. More computationally demanding than Detail 2D. Produces a code-check report to EN 1992 or ACI 318.

A free, read-only application that allows anyone to open and inspect an IDEA StatiCa Connection or Detail model and its results without holding a paid licence. Engineers can share their .ideacon or .ideadet files with clients, fabricators, detailers, checkers, and EOR for review. The viewer shows the 3D connection geometry, applied loads, CBFEM or CSFM results, component utilisations, and the code-check report. It cannot modify the model or re-run the analysis. Removes the barrier to third-party review of IDEA StatiCa calculations.

A curated online and in-product database of pre-designed, code-checked connection models for common steel joint configurations - end plates, fin plates, base plates, moment connections, hollow section joints, and others. Engineers can download a library connection as a starting point, adapt the geometry and loads to their specific project, and re-run the code-check. Firms can also build and share their own internal connection libraries to standardise preferred details and reduce design time across teams and projects.

Pre-built connection configurations within IDEA StatiCa Connection where the geometry is defined by named parameters - plate thickness, bolt diameter, number of bolt rows, weld throat, etc. - rather than fixed dimensions. The engineer selects the appropriate template (e.g. extended end plate, column base, welded T-stub), inputs the project-specific parameters, and IDEA StatiCa automatically builds the FE model and runs the code-check. Templates speed up routine design, ensure consistent modelling practice across a team, and can be saved to the Connection Library for reuse.

A new IDEA StatiCa application (currently in Beta, free to all users) for designing and code-checking reinforced concrete cross-sections at Ultimate Limit State: capacity (N-My-Mz interaction), shear, and torsion. Built on a finite element core and intended to replace the legacy RCS product. The first IDEA StatiCa application to support EN 1992-1-1:2023 (second-generation Eurocode 2). Every check shows the full equation with substituted values and the relevant code clause reference, in both the interactive view and the exported report.
